directions: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Blakeney Red is a vigorous, self-fertile perry pear, but still crops more heavily with a second variety for cross-pollination. One of the most widely planted traditional English perry pears, originating in the Forest of Dean area of Gloucestershire, it produces a heavy, reliable crop of small, red-blushed pears on a large, vigorous, long-lived tree, valued by perry makers for moderate tannin and good juice yield that blends well in traditional West Country perry production. Unlike many perry pears, it is self-fertile, making it a more forgiving choice for an orchard with limited space for a dedicated pollinator tree, though a second variety still improves cropping. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, and let it sweat in a pile for a few days before milling and pressing.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

directions: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Barland is an exceptionally slow tree to reach bearing age, sometimes taking well over a decade. A classic Herefordshire perry pear long prized for producing exceptionally high-tannin, astringent juice that gives finished perry real structure and aging potential, it is considered one of the finest true perry pears despite, or because of, fruit far too harsh and bitter for fresh eating. Its notoriously slow growth to first bearing has always made it a tree planted for a future generation rather than quick reward, a tradition reflected in the old West Country saying about planting pears for one's heirs. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften and mellow, then mill and press for perry.

directions: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Thorn is a reliably productive, widely grown traditional Gloucestershire perry pear. One of the classic Three Counties perry pears traditionally grown across Gloucestershire, Herefordshire, and Worcestershire, it produces a reliable crop of small, hard, astringent fruit prized for well-balanced tannin and good juice yield, and it remains a component of a number of well-regarded commercial English perry blends. Like most true perry pears it is grown solely for fermenting into perry rather than fresh eating, and it shares the group's characteristically slow growth to first significant bearing. Harvest the hard fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften, then mill and press for perry.

directions: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Hendre Huffcap is one of the more precocious perry pears, bearing somewhat sooner than many other traditional varieties. A well-regarded Herefordshire perry pear producing large, elongated, aromatic fruit for the type, it yields fragrant, medium-tannin juice that makes for a softer, more approachable perry than the harshest bittersharp varieties, contributing floral aromatics valued by perry makers seeking a more delicate finished blend. Its comparatively earlier bearing age and good, consistent yields have made it one of the more commercially popular traditional perry pears for new plantings. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften and develop aroma, then mill and press for perry.

directions: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Taynton Squash is among the oldest documented perry pear cultivars and one of the largest, most long-lived trees in the group. Named for the village of Taynton in Gloucestershire and documented since at least the seventeenth century, it is considered one of the oldest surviving named perry pear cultivars in England, producing a reliable crop of small, mid-tannin fruit on a tree capable of growing to an immense size and living for well over a century under good conditions. Its ancient pedigree and reliable cropping have kept it in cultivation in traditional Gloucestershire perry orchards continuously since long before named fruit varieties were commonly propagated by grafting elsewhere in Europe. Harvest the hard, astringent fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften, then mill and press for perry.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste
